notes.1a: (i) All candidates were able to select the jelly coating for the egg cell. Many candidates, because they were looking for ‘is very small’, chose ‘is very thin’ instead.
notes.1aii: This question was well answered, with most candidates correctly labelling the parts. Candidates should ensure that label lines touch the parts being labelled.
notes.1b: (i) Most candidates were aware that the nucleus is the largest of the three structures. It was less well known that the gene is the smallest.
notes.1bii: Some candidates gave the correct response, but a common misconception was to name protein as the molecule.
notes.1c: Many candidates gave the answer as a specialised tissue, rather than cells. A common error was to write cilia rather than ciliated cell.
notes.2a: This question was well answered and most candidates were able to identify the structure as a sensory neurone.
notes.2b: (i) Most candidates could recall that the synapse is a junction between two neurones.
notes.2bii: Many candidates knew that a nerve impulse is an electrical signal. A number of candidates gave the parts of the ‘stimulus–response’ chain itself, rather than the impulse.
notes.2c: This question was well answered and candidates clearly understood the structure and role of the human nervous system.
notes.2d: This question asked for chemical elements to be named, but many candidates incorrectly gave amino acids.
notes.2e: This question was well answered, although some were confused by having to draw two lines to the box labelled glucose. �PAGE�25
notes.3a: Most candidates were able to relate cell structures to functions. A few candidates thought that photosynthesis, rather than respiration, releases energy.
notes.3b: (i) This question compared meiosis and mitosis. Those candidates that correctly identified meiosis as producing gametes were able to correctly tick more boxes.
notes.3bii: Although most candidates understood the role of X and Y chromosomes, many did not give the pairs of chromosomes in the boxes. Candidates would benefit from carefully reading the headings in tables.
notes.4a: This question asked for a definition of variation. Many candidates gave causes and examples of differences rather than a clear definition.
notes.4b: (i) The majority of candidates correctly read a frequency value off the histogram.
notes.4bii: The majority of candidates selected the correct hand span range.
notes.4c: Candidates were required to state the type of variation and then give evidence. It is important in data handling questions to refer to the data given in the question.
notes.5a: (i) The majority of candidates correctly labelled the testes.
notes.5aii: Many candidates knew that oestrogen controls the development of secondary sexual characteristics in girls.
notes.5iii: Most candidates were able to sort the characteristics correctly, but some incorrectly placed pubic hair and underarm hair in both columns.
notes.5b: Candidates gave quite detailed answers for the effect of adrenaline, but many of them were not biological.
notes.6a: (i) A ‘define’ question requires a precise answer rather than a discussion. Some candidates were confused about the role of energy in respiration. Energy is released but is not produced in respiration.
notes.6aii: It is important to read the whole question carefully. Some candidates quoted the products of anaerobic respiration in muscle and yeast.
notes.6iii: Many candidates were able to give at least one difference between anaerobic respiration in yeast and muscle cells.
notes.6b: (i) Nearly all candidates calculated correctly, with just a few forgetting to round to a whole number.
notes.6bii: While many candidates understood that aerobic respiration releases more energy, answers often contained errors in the description of energy. Many were aware of the problems of lactic acid build up in muscles.
notes.6c: This was a challenging question. Most candidates were able to work out the increase, but some were unable to convert it to a percentage.
notes.6d: This question was generally well answered, although a small number of candidates thought they had to give the corrected sentences, rather than the incorrect words. �PAGE�26
notes.7a: (i) Most candidates were able to describe the growth of the tomato seedlings.
notes.7iii: This question was well answered with excellent explanations of why seedlings need light, showing the connections between light, photosynthesis and growth.
notes.7iv: Few candidates understood that roots respond to light by growing away from it.
notes.7b: The question specifies conditions for the germination of seeds, not the growth of seedlings. Most candidates incorrectly gave light as an essential condition.
notes.7c: This was a challenging question. Most answers described the role of xylem and root hair cells, rather than turgid cells.
notes.8a: Candidates confidently identified the parts of the eye and completed the table.
notes.8b: This question was generally well answered and the pupil reflex was well understood. �PAGE�27
notes.key_messages:
Candidates would benefit from reading the question carefully, particularly noting how many answers they
need to give. For example, if the question asks for chromosomes or Petri dishes and is for more than one
mark, then more than one answer is required.
notes.general_comments:
Candidates should make sure labels are drawn clearly and that they touch the structure being labelled.
There was continued improvement in classifying information into categories.
